clap builds the whole command line from a struct: flags, arguments, subcommands, `--help` and error messages. Your doc comments become the help text.

<Remember>Describe your command line as a struct, derive `Parser`, and call `Cli::parse()`.</Remember>

## The same tool in Go, with the standard flag package

<Files guide="clap" dir="go" files={["main.go"]} run="go" lang="go" />

The last command puts `-verbose` after the text. Go's `flag` package stops reading flags at the first argument that is not a flag ([docs](https://pkg.go.dev/flag)), so it did not complain and did not turn verbose mode on.

- **Doc comments** (`///`) become the help text. The two `--help` runs above are built from them, so the description sits next to the code it describes.
- **Types do the checking.** `priority: u8` is why `-p abc` is rejected with a clear message, and why `-p 300` is too (try it below). A `u8` allows 0 to 255, so "between 1 and 3" is still a rule you write yourself. `default_value_t = 2` shows up as `[default: 2]` in the help.
- **Subcommands are an enum, so a `match` without a `_` arm must cover every one.** Add a `Done { id: u32 }` variant and leave `main` alone, and the build fails ([Enums](/learn/enums/#match-must-cover-every-variant) explains why):

<Session guide="clap" run="new-command" />

- **Global flags.** A flag on the top-level struct has to come before the subcommand unless it is marked `global = true`, which lets `--verbose` go anywhere. The first run on this page uses it after `add`. The session below takes `, global = true` out of a copy and runs it again: after `add` it is refused, and before `add` it works. Go's `flag` (above) and Python's `argparse` (in the table below) also need it first.

<Session guide="clap" run="global" />
- **Exit codes.** In these runs a usage error exited with code 2 and `--help` with 0. The clap docs for [`Error::exit`](https://docs.rs/clap/4.6.7/clap/error/struct.Error.html) say the same: status 2 when it prints to stderr, 0 when it prints to stdout.

## The same job in your language

Where the image has a parser that comes with the language or its runtime, I wrote the same to-do tool with it. The other cells only name the usual libraries; I did not run those.

| Language | Built in, and run for this page | Libraries people use (named, not run) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | `std::env::args` is only the raw list of strings ([Arguments](/learn/env-time-process/#arguments)) | clap |
| Go | `flag` (the program above) | cobra |
| Python | `argparse` | Typer, Click |
| TypeScript | `util.parseArgs`, built into Node (the version is the first line of the runs below) | commander, yargs |
| Java | nothing run | picocli |
| Kotlin | nothing run | Clikt |
| C# | nothing run | System.CommandLine (a NuGet package, per Microsoft's docs) |
| C | `getopt` (POSIX, from the C library; run with glibc, the GNU C library) | none named |
| C++ | nothing run | CLI11, cxxopts |

What the runs showed:

<Session guide="clap" run="langs" />

- `argparse` checks the number for you (`type=int`), like clap, and its subparsers also need `--verbose` before `add`.
- `parseArgs` and `getopt` hand back text. The number check and the "invalid priority" message are code I wrote. Neither knows about subcommands, so `--verbose` and `-v` were accepted after the text. For `getopt` that is glibc's default (glibc is the GNU C library): it moves non-option arguments to the end as it scans, and `POSIXLY_CORRECT` or a leading `+` in the option string stops at the first one ([man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/getopt.3.html)).

## Try it yourself

Run each command in the project. The session below was run in the image.

1. `cargo run -- --version`. It prints `todo-cli 0.1.0`, from `#[command(version)]` and the version in `Cargo.toml`.
2. `cargo run -- add "learn clap" -p 300`. Look for `300 is not in 0..=255`: the `u8` type is the rule.
3. `cargo run -- ad "learn clap"`. clap rejects the unknown subcommand and adds a tip that `add` is similar.
4. `cargo run -- add "-draft"`. The text starts with a dash, so clap reads `-d` as a flag and says to use `-- -d`; with `--` before it, the same text is accepted as the task.

<Session guide="clap" run="try" />
